title: Exertional rhabdomyolysis
why_this_matters: Exertional muscle breakdown occurs in working dogs and is a listed complication of canine heatstroke, but the canine evidence is thin [1][2][6].

what_changes_from_human.point: Canine exertional rhabdomyolysis has been studied with creatine kinase and myoglobin in endurance sled dogs, which correlated strongly [1].
Human hydration and outpatient rules are built on human cohorts and are not established for dogs [3][4][5].

recognition: In endurance sled dogs, myoglobin and creatine kinase were higher in dogs with clinical rhabdomyolysis than in normal dogs and were strongly correlated (R = 0.91). Rhabdomyolysis appeared to occur early in endurance activity [1].
Rhabdomyolysis is a listed complication of canine heatstroke, along with acute kidney injury [6].
management: Cell-free DNA was not a useful marker in sled dogs, unlike myoglobin and creatine kinase [1].
In trained search and rescue dogs, CK and AST did not change after 20 minutes of submaximal search work, consistent with conditioning protecting against enzyme changes [2].
Human data, context only: acute kidney injury is a main complication, hydration is the commonest treatment, and outpatient care was safe in one cohort when admission creatinine was normal [3][4][5].

TODO: canine signs, treatment and the link to exertional hypoglycemia. Only two canine studies were retrieved and none tests a treatment. Do not extrapolate the human hydration or outpatient findings.

takeaway: In a working dog that collapses or is stiff after hard work, think muscle breakdown as well as heat, and hand the dog to a veterinarian who can check muscle and kidney values.
